content:
There's an old saying in photography that the best camera is the one you have with you. Of course, the iPhone is the camera most of us carry around most of the time, which is a huge advantage for shooting kids, social occasions, and the like. But an ongoing video project revealed another benefit to me.

I love taking walks around London in the early evening, and I often shoot photos and short videos with my iPhone. At first, I was just doing it for fun, then I realised these short clips could serve as b-roll (空鏡) material for a video project…

My current project is experimental, testing whether shooting in Cinematic Mode (電影模式) is viable—which is what I lamented earlier about the company seemingly discontinuing development of the feature. I'll share it with you next week once it's done.

I'm using a very specific format that requires very short landscape b-roll clips cut between interview segments. In principle, these clips could be shot anywhere in London, but since the main shoot location is by the river, I really wanted all the b-roll to be of the Thames. I needed four such shots, and after searching through my iPhone video library, I quickly found suitable clips.

The clips above also highlight another benefit. If there are potentially identifiable people in the frame, I go up to them afterwards and show them the clip, asking permission to use it. (This isn't a legal requirement in the UK, but I think it's good manners.) They very often ask for a copy. If they're on iPhone, AirDrop is quick and easy; Android users can fall back on WhatsApp.

The iPhone's image stabilisation is particularly useful for casual shots grabbed while walking, since these are all handheld. Although I do try to brace myself against walls, railings, lamp posts, etc., the footage is generally very stable straight out of camera, almost as if shot on a tripod. (When I expect to be filming while walking, I also bring a small GorillaPod.)

Another huge advantage of the iPhone is its grab-and-go nature. If I had to manually set exposure, white balance, ND filters, etc., I probably wouldn't bother, especially when I'm with someone—the time required is too intrusive. But just asking them to wait around 20 seconds or so doesn't feel like a real interruption to the walk.

If I want to linger somewhere for a while, it's also easy to shoot timelapse video with the iPhone. Set it to start, stop recording whenever, and the iPhone automatically adjusts to output a clip of the right length. Back in my old flat, I used to regularly prop my iPhone by the window at sunset, start a timelapse, and get on with things. A few of those later became excellent b-roll for video projects.

Of course, if you pixel-peep, the limitations of the iPhone's tiny sensor start to show, particularly in low light. But in an age where most YouTube videos are watched on phones or laptops, the quality is more than sufficient in most cases.

Whether video shot in Cinematic Mode meets the same standard is harder to say—you can help me judge next week. But overall, I'm pleasantly surprised by what such a fully featured camera is capable of when it's sitting in my pocket.
